body_markdown:
California employer payroll taxes in 2026 (UI, ETT, SDI and withholding)
A California employer deals with four state payroll taxes. It pays unemployment insurance (UI) and the Employment Training Tax (ETT) itself, and it withholds State Disability Insurance (SDI) and personal income tax (PIT) from employee wages. The Employment Development Department (EDD) receives all four and publishes the rates, wage limits, due dates and penalties that apply.
Which payroll taxes does a California employer pay or withhold?
California has four state payroll taxes, of which unemployment insurance (UI) and the Employment Training Tax (ETT) are paid by employers, and State Disability Insurance (SDI) and personal income tax (PIT) are withheld from employee wages.


Wages are generally subject to all four taxes unless the law says otherwise, and EDD points to Information Sheets DE 231TE and DE 231TP for the types of employment and payments that are not. A tax-rated employer pays into the UI fund, while nonprofit and public-entity employers may instead choose the reimbursable method. Paid Family Leave (PFL) is a component of the SDI program, not a separate California employer tax.
When must a new employer register with the EDD?
As EDD states it, a California business that hires employees and pays more than $100 in wages in a calendar quarter must register as an employer with the Employment Development Department (EDD) within 15 days. EDD’s Employer’s Guide counts the 15 days from paying wages over $100. Wages counted toward the $100 include checks, cash, electronic payments, payment-app payments and the cash value of noncash payments such as meals and lodging.


A household employer (a person who hires household workers in or around the home) registers within 15 days after paying $750 or more in cash wages in a calendar quarter, and noncash wages do not count toward that $750. A business run from the home, such as a daycare, registers as a commercial employer.
How do I register for a California employer payroll tax account?
The fastest way to register is online through EDD’s e-Services for Business, where the employer enrolls, logs in, selects New Employer and completes the online application. The paper alternative is the Commercial Employer Account Registration and Update Form (DE 1). As of November 2026, EDD says mail-in registrations may take 10 to 14 days to process, and some cases, such as accounts with tax exemptions or special coverage requirements, may take longer.


EDD tells a business employer to gather these items before registering. They include the names and Social Security numbers of all responsible parties, the physical and mailing address, the phone number and email address, the nine-digit Federal Employer Identification Number (FEIN), any previous EDD account, the date of the first payroll when wages exceeded $100 and, for corporations, LLCs, LLPs and LPs, the exact legal name registered with the California Secretary of State.


After registration EDD issues an eight-digit employer payroll tax account number, which EDD says is needed for all interactions with EDD, including filing returns and submitting payments.
What is the California unemployment insurance rate for a new employer?
For 2026, California UI tax applies to the first $7,000 of each employee’s wages in a calendar year, and EDD assigns a new employer a 3.4 percent UI rate for two to three years. Whether the period is two years or three depends on when the employer meets the criteria under section 982(b) of the California Unemployment Insurance Code. 3.4 percent of $7,000 is $238 per employee per year, the amount shown in EDD’s own worked example.
What is the California unemployment insurance taxable wage base?
The California UI taxable wage base is $7,000 per employee per calendar year, for 2026 and for 2027. Once an employee reaches $7,000 in a year, no further UI is due on that employee’s wages for the year, as EDD’s taxable wages page shows, but the employer still reports total subject wages, according to EDD’s Employer’s Guide. As of November 2026, the maximum UI tax at a Schedule F+ rate is $434 per employee per year, which is the highest rate of 6.2 percent on $7,000.
How does California set my unemployment insurance rate after the new-employer period?
After the new-employer period, a tax-rated employer’s UI rate comes from an experience-rating schedule, and the 2026 schedule, Schedule F+, runs from 1.5 percent to 6.2 percent. Schedule F+ is Schedule F plus a 15 percent emergency surcharge, and on the $7,000 wage limit the range is $105 to $434 per employee. Each tax-rated employer has a UI reserve account, a nonmonetary record of benefit charges and credits that EDD uses to determine the rate, as EDD’s tax-rated employer page describes.


EDD mails the Notice of Contribution Rates and Statement of UI Reserve Account (DE 2088) in December with a mailing date of December 31. As of November 2026, an employer has 60 days from the issued or mailing date to protest any item on it except SDI and ETT, which are set by law, and EDD allows an extension of up to 60 days for good cause if the employer asks in writing before the deadline.


An employer subject to section 977(c) of the California Unemployment Insurance Code must pay at the highest rate provided by law plus an additional 2 percent, and EDD says changing business ownership or entity solely to obtain a lower UI rate is not allowed.
What is the Employment Training Tax, and does my business owe it?
The Employment Training Tax is 0.1 percent of the first $7,000 of each employee’s wages for an employer whose UI reserve account balance is zero or positive, and an employer with a negative balance does not pay it. For 2026 and for 2027, ETT is an employer-paid tax at 0.1 percent, so the most an employer pays is $7 per employee per year. An employer with a negative balance sees ETT as 0.0 percent on its DE 2088, and an employer that must pay the maximum UI rate plus 2 percent under section 977(c) does not owe ETT either. An ETT rate cannot be protested.
What is California SDI, and is there a wage cap?
California SDI is funded by a payroll deduction from employee wages, which the employer withholds and pays to EDD, with no taxable wage limit. For 2026 the SDI withholding rate is 1.3 percent of all wages, with no taxable wage limit since January 1, 2024, and EDD states that the 2027 rate is 1.4 percent, according to EDD’s rates page. The rate is the same for all employees, is calculated annually under section 984 of the California Unemployment Insurance Code based on the balance in the SDI Fund and the amount of disbursements and wages paid, and cannot be protested.
What do I owe for California Paid Family Leave?
Paid Family Leave (PFL) is part of the SDI program, so an employer handles it by withholding SDI contributions from employee wages and sending them to EDD, not by paying a separate PFL tax. EDD funds PFL benefits through SDI contributions withheld from paychecks, which most often appear as “CASDI” on paystubs. EDD lists three employer duties for PFL, which are to collect employee payroll contributions and send them to EDD, give employees information about benefit programs and respond to employee claims.


A Voluntary Plan (VP) is an employer alternative to SDI, a private short-term disability insurance option that EDD says must provide all the benefits of SDI and at least one better benefit and cannot cost employees more than SDI.
How much do California payroll taxes cost for each employee I hire?
At a new employer’s 3.4 percent UI rate and 0.1 percent ETT rate, the California payroll taxes an employer pays come to $245 a year for an employee paid at least $7,000, because UI and ETT each apply only to the first $7,000 of wages in a calendar year, according to EDD’s rates page. SDI and PIT come out of the employee’s pay and are not paid by the employer on top of wages.

Federal unemployment tax (FUTA) applies in addition to these California taxes. For 2026 the FUTA tax rate is 6.0 percent on the first $7,000 paid to each employee; an employer that pays state unemployment tax in full, on time and on the same wages can take a credit of up to 5.4 percent, which leaves 0.6 percent; the state wage base may be different. California has an outstanding federal unemployment loan, and EDD’s FUTA page for wages paid in 2025 says the credit was reduced by 1.2 percent for the 2025 tax year, which EDD says means employers pay an extra $84 per employee for 2025. Which states are FUTA credit reduction states for 2026 is not final until after November 10, 2026, when the Department of Labor announces them, so check Schedule A (Form 940) and DOL’s FUTA credit reductions page after that date.
How do I withhold California personal income tax from employee pay?
An employer withholds California PIT from most employee wages based on the Employee’s Withholding Allowance Certificate (DE 4) the employee has on file, and there is no taxable wage limit and no maximum. Each new employee must complete both the federal Form W-4, which is used for federal income tax, and the state Employee’s Withholding Allowance Certificate (DE 4), which is used for California PIT withholding. If an employee does not give a properly completed DE 4, the employer withholds as if the employee were single with zero withholding allowances, though an employer may keep using a valid certificate already on file for that employee. An employer does not withhold California PIT from an employee who files a DE 4 marked exempt, unless the Franchise Tax Board sends written notice to withhold at a special rate. A DE 4 claiming exempt status is valid only during the calendar year it was filed, so the employer withholds again in the next year unless the employee gives a new DE 4 claiming exempt status by February 15 of that year, according to EDD’s Employer’s Guide.


California publishes two withholding methods, Method A, a wage bracket table method limited to wages or salaries under $1 million, and Method B, an exact calculation method. As of November 2026, EDD’s rates page posts the 2026 and 2027 schedules.


A California resident’s wages are subject to PIT withholding whether the services are performed in California or another state. If another jurisdiction also requires withholding on those wages, the employer withholds that amount and then California only for the amount by which California’s withholding exceeds it. A nonresident who works partly in California has withholding only on the California share, which is the portion of total working days employed in California or, for pay that depends on the volume of business transacted, the portion of earnings received for business transacted in California.
What rate applies to bonuses and other supplemental wages in California?
When supplemental wages are paid separately from regular wages, an employer may withhold California PIT at a flat 10.23 percent on bonuses and stock options and 6.6 percent on other supplemental wages, or may use the combined-wages method. Supplemental wages include bonuses, overtime pay, sales awards, commissions, stock options, vacation pay and dismissal or severance pay, and those paid at the same time as regular wages are added to the regular wages and withheld on the payroll period.


Under the combined-wages method, the employer computes PIT on the combined regular and supplemental wages using the schedules and subtracts the PIT already withheld from regular wages. The flat-rate option withholds without allowing for withholding allowances and is the employer’s choice. As of November 2026, EDD’s Information Sheet DE 231PS and the 2026 Employer’s Guide give the same two flat rates.
When are California payroll tax returns and deposits due?
California UI and ETT contributions and the DE 9 and DE 9C returns for a quarter are due on the first day after the quarter ends and are delinquent if not filed or paid by the last timely date, which is April 30, 2026 for the first quarter, July 31 for the second, November 2 for the third and February 1, 2027 for the fourth, according to EDD’s payroll tax calendar. If the last timely date falls on a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, the next business day is the last timely date.


Every quarter an employer files both the Quarterly Contribution Return and Report of Wages (DE 9), which reconciles reported wages and paid taxes, and its Continuation (DE 9C), which lists individual employee wages and PIT wages. Both are required even when no wages were paid.


Electronic payments are timely by settlement date. The payment must be initiated by the last timely date (an ACH debit before 3 p.m. Pacific time) and settle by the timely settlement date, which for 2026 is May 1, August 3 and November 3 and, for the fourth quarter, February 2, 2027, according to EDD’s Employer’s Guide.

Do I have to file and pay California payroll taxes electronically?
All employers, including out-of-state employers, must submit employment tax returns, wage reports and payroll tax deposits to EDD electronically.


As of November 2026, the penalties for not complying are $50 per return (DE 9, DE 3D and DE 3HW), $20 per wage item (DE 9C and DE 3BHW) and 15 percent of the amount due for payments (DE 88), and they apply even when a paper return reports no wages. An employer can request a waiver using form DE 1245W, which is valid for one year, and EDD says a denial cannot be appealed.
How do I report new hires in California?
An employer must report every new or rehired employee who works in California to EDD’s New Employee Registry, using the Report of New Employee(s) (DE 34), within 20 calendar days of the start-of-work date, which is the first day the employee performed services for pay, according to EDD’s new employee registry page. The duty applies regardless of the number of employees, to part-time and seasonal workers even if the person stops working before day 20, and to employees who live outside California. A rehire is an employee who was separated from the same employer for at least 60 consecutive days.


An employer reports through e-Services for Business or on paper. As of November 2026, EDD says a penalty of $24 for each unreported employee may be charged, and $490 may be charged if the employer and employee intentionally agree not to supply the required information or to supply a false or incomplete report.
Which notices must a California employer post or give to employees?
A California employer must post the EDD notice that tells employees about their UI, Disability Insurance (DI) and PFL rights where employees easily see it, and must give employees pamphlets and notices at set points, according to EDD’s required notices page.


* Post the notice EDD sends after registration, which is DE 1857A for UI, DI and PFL, DE 1857D for UI only, or DE 1858 for DI and PFL only.
* Give employees the pamphlets when needed, which are For Your Benefit (DE 2320) when discharging, laying off or placing an employee on leave, the DI brochure (DE 2515) and the PFL brochure (DE 2511).
* Give the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) notice twice a year if the employer is subject to and required to provide UI, once within one week before, after or during the time the annual wage summary (such as Form W-2) is provided and again in March. The notice must be handed over or mailed, though the March one may be sent electronically.
* Give written notice immediately when an employee is fired, laid off, takes a leave of absence or has a job status change. EDD says none is needed for a voluntary quit, a promotion, a demotion or work stopped by a trade dispute.
What happens if I file or pay California payroll taxes late?
EDD charges a penalty of 15 percent plus interest on late payroll tax payments. The penalty is 15 percent of the portion of the payment that is late. As of November 2026, EDD’s interest rate on overdue taxes is 7 percent for July 1 to December 31, 2026, and EDD adjusts the rate twice a year. Interest compounds daily on unpaid tax, interest and certain penalties, and EDD says it cannot waive or cancel interest. If a balance stays unpaid, a state tax lien may be recorded.


EDD also charges penalty and interest on late reports. If a DE 9C is not submitted on time, EDD issues a written demand, and if it is still not submitted within 15 days of the demand date, EDD charges a penalty of $20 for each unreported employee plus interest unless there is good cause for the delay.
What changes for California employers in 2027?
EDD has already published 2027 figures for UI, ETT, SDI and PIT withholding, and the SDI withholding rate for 2027 is 1.4 percent, up from 1.3 percent for 2026. As of November 2026, the 2027 figures on EDD’s rates page and employer news page are these.
